\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{amsmath}
\usepackage{booktabs}

\title{High-Intensity Interval Training in Cardiac Rehabilitation After Myocardial Infarction:\\A Multicentre Randomised Controlled Trial}
\author{S.~L.~Adeyemi, K.~Fournier, J.~H.~Rhee, and M.~Castellanos}
\date{March 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\section{Introduction}
Exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation reduces cardiovascular mortality
and hospital readmission after myocardial infarction, yet the optimal
intensity of the exercise stimulus remains contested. Traditional
programmes rely on moderate-intensity continuous training, typically
performed at 60--70\% of peak heart rate, because of long-standing
concerns about the safety of vigorous exertion in patients with recent
coronary events. Over the past decade, high-intensity interval training
(HIIT), consisting of short bouts at 85--95\% of peak heart rate
interspersed with active recovery, has emerged as a time-efficient
alternative that produces larger gains in cardiorespiratory fitness in
stable coronary populations.

The evidence base, however, has important gaps. Most HIIT trials in
cardiac rehabilitation have been single-centre studies with fewer than
one hundred participants, follow-up limited to the duration of the
training programme, and surrogate endpoints such as peak oxygen uptake
rather than clinical events. Whether the larger fitness gains translate
into fewer recurrent events, and whether the intervention remains safe
when delivered at scale across centres with differing protocols and
staffing, are the questions that matter for guideline committees.

The present trial was designed to answer these questions. We randomised
patients entering cardiac rehabilitation after myocardial infarction to
either HIIT or standard moderate-intensity continuous training, stratified
by centre and by left ventricular ejection fraction, and followed them
for clinical events beyond the end of the structured programme. The
primary hypothesis was that HIIT would reduce the composite of
cardiovascular death, recurrent myocardial infarction, and
hospitalisation for heart failure compared with standard training.

\section{Methods}
\subsection{Design and Participants}
The trial was conducted at nine cardiac rehabilitation centres across
three countries between January 2021 and June 2024. Adults aged 30 to 75
years were eligible if they had experienced a myocardial infarction
within the preceding eight weeks, had completed revascularisation when
indicated, and were clinically stable at enrolment. Key exclusion criteria
were uncontrolled arrhythmia, severe aortic stenosis, inability to
perform an exercise test, and participation in another interventional
trial. All participants provided written informed consent, and the
protocol was approved by the ethics committee at each centre.

Randomisation was performed centrally in permuted blocks of variable
size, stratified by centre and by baseline ejection fraction above or
below 40\%. Allocation was concealed from the recruiting clinicians until
after enrolment. Because of the nature of the intervention, participants
and exercise staff could not be blinded, but all outcome events were
adjudicated by an independent committee blinded to treatment assignment.

An independent data and safety monitoring board reviewed the accumulating
data after every 100 primary endpoint events were projected to have
accrued, with prespecified stopping guidelines for both efficacy and
harm. Two interim reviews recommended continuation without modification
of the protocol.

\subsection{Interventions}
Participants in both groups attended supervised exercise sessions three
times per week for twelve weeks, followed by a home-based maintenance
phase with monthly telephone coaching. The HIIT group performed a
ten-minute warm-up, then four intervals of four minutes at 85--95\% of
peak heart rate separated by three-minute active recovery periods at
60--70\% of peak heart rate, and a five-minute cool-down. The control
group performed 40 minutes of continuous exercise at 60--70\% of peak
heart rate. Heart rate was monitored continuously during every supervised
session, and exercise intensity was titrated weekly against a repeat
submaximal test at week four.

Both groups received identical counselling on diet, smoking cessation,
and medication adherence. Concomitant therapy, including beta-blockers,
statins, and antiplatelet agents, followed contemporary guidelines and
was recorded at every study visit.

\subsection{Outcomes}
The primary endpoint was the composite of cardiovascular death,
recurrent myocardial infarction, and hospitalisation for heart failure.
Secondary endpoints included peak oxygen uptake measured by
cardiopulmonary exercise testing, health-related quality of life, and
each component of the primary composite. Serious adverse events were
defined as events that were fatal, life-threatening, or required
hospitalisation, and were reviewed by an independent safety board every
three months.

\subsection{Statistical Analysis}
The trial was powered to detect a 30\% relative reduction in the primary
composite with 85\% power at a two-sided significance level of 5\%,
assuming a control-group event rate of 14\% and allowing for 8\% loss to
follow-up. Time-to-event outcomes were analysed with Cox proportional
hazards models stratified by centre, and continuous outcomes with linear
mixed models adjusted for the baseline value. All analyses followed the
intention-to-treat principle, and missing outcome data were handled by
multiple imputation with twenty imputed datasets.

All effect estimates are reported with 95\% confidence intervals, and no
formal adjustment for multiplicity was applied to the secondary
endpoints, which are therefore interpreted as supportive. The trial is
registered, and the statistical analysis plan was finalised before the
database was locked for the primary analysis.

\section{Results}
\subsection{Participant Flow and Baseline Characteristics}
Between January 2021 and March 2023, 893 patients were assessed for
eligibility across the nine centres. Of these, 211 were ineligible, most
commonly because of uncontrolled arrhythmia or inability to perform an
exercise test, and 70 declined to participate. The remaining 612 patients
were randomised, 306 to high-intensity interval training and 306 to
moderate-intensity continuous training. Baseline characteristics were
well balanced between the groups: the mean age was 58.4 years, 24\% were
women, the median time from infarction to randomisation was 5.1 weeks,
and 18\% had an ejection fraction below 40\%.

Adherence to the supervised phase was high and similar between groups,
with a median of 33 of 36 scheduled sessions attended in the HIIT group
and 34 of 36 in the control group. During the maintenance phase, 78\% of
participants in both groups reported exercising at least twice per week
at the six-month telephone contact.

\subsection{Training Response}
Peak oxygen uptake increased more in the HIIT group than in the control
group, with a between-group difference of 2.4~mL/kg/min in favour of HIIT
at the end of the supervised phase, a difference that was attenuated but
still significant at the final follow-up. Resting heart rate and blood
pressure changed similarly in the two groups, and there were no
differences in quality-of-life scores at any time point.

\subsection{Clinical Events}
The median follow-up was 18 months from randomisation. A primary
composite endpoint event occurred in 41 of 306 patients in the HIIT group
and in 53 of 306 patients in the control group. The hazard ratio for the
primary composite was 0.75 with a 95\% confidence interval of 0.50 to
1.13, corresponding to a relative reduction of 23\% after adjustment for
the stratification factors, with the adjustment performed as prespecified
in the statistical analysis plan; the nominal p-value was 0.17. The
components of the composite showed consistent directions: recurrent
myocardial infarction occurred in 22 versus 31 patients, hospitalisation
for heart failure in 13 versus 16, and cardiovascular death in 6 versus
6 patients. Table~\ref{tab:events} summarises the clinical events.
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Clinical events during follow-up, by treatment group.}
\label{tab:events}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Endpoint & HIIT ($n=306$) & Control ($n=306$) \\
\midrule
Primary composite & 41 & 53 \\
Recurrent myocardial infarction & 22 & 31 \\
Heart-failure hospitalisation & 13 & 16 \\
Cardiovascular death & 6 & 6 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{Safety}
Serious adverse events occurred in 13 of 306 participants in the HIIT
group (4.2\%) and in 19 of 306 participants in the control group (6.1\%).
No serious adverse event was judged by the blinded safety board to be
definitely related to the exercise intervention. Two events in the HIIT
group, one episode of sustained ventricular tachycardia during a session
and one syncopal episode two hours after a session, were judged possibly
related; both patients recovered fully and completed the programme.
Non-serious musculoskeletal complaints were more frequent with HIIT,
affecting 11\% of participants versus 7\% in the control group, and led
to temporary modification of the exercise prescription in most cases.

\subsection{Subgroup and Sensitivity Analyses}
The effect on the primary composite was consistent across prespecified
subgroups defined by age, sex, ejection fraction, and centre volume,
with no significant interaction. Sensitivity analyses restricted to the
per-protocol population, and analyses using recurrent-event models that
counted multiple hospitalisations, produced estimates compatible with
the primary analysis.

\section{Discussion}
In this multicentre trial, high-intensity interval training produced a
relative reduction of about a quarter in the composite of cardiovascular
death, recurrent infarction, and heart-failure hospitalisation, but the
confidence interval was wide and included unity, so the trial does not
by itself settle the clinical superiority of HIIT over standard
rehabilitation training. The direction and magnitude of the point
estimate are consistent with the meta-analytic signal from smaller
trials, and the safety findings are reassuring: serious adverse events
were numerically less frequent with HIIT than with conventional
training, and no event was definitely attributable to the intervention.

The fitness findings confirm the smaller efficacy literature at
multicentre scale: the between-group difference in peak oxygen uptake
was clinically meaningful at the end of the supervised phase and
remained detectable, though attenuated, after the maintenance phase. The
attenuation mirrors the adherence data and underlines the central
challenge of exercise interventions, namely that physiological gains
fade when supervision is withdrawn.

The trial also speaks to an ongoing debate about implementation. Critics
of HIIT in rehabilitation have argued that the protocol is too complex
for routine programmes and that its benefits demonstrated in research
settings will not survive contact with ordinary clinical staffing. Our
experience suggests otherwise: the protocol was delivered at nine
centres with widely varying resources, the titration rules were followed
with high fidelity, and the between-centre heterogeneity in the training
response was small. The resource comparison is less favourable than the
popularity of HIIT suggests, however, because the continuous heart-rate
monitoring that the protocol requires adds equipment and staff time that
not all programmes currently budget for.

The equivalence of the two groups in quality-of-life outcomes deserves
comment, since patient preference is often cited as a reason to offer
interval formats. Participants in both groups reported high satisfaction,
and the enjoyment subscales did not differ, suggesting that in a
supervised setting with careful titration the format of the exercise
stimulus is not the main determinant of the patient's experience.

Several limitations temper the interpretation. The trial was powered for
a larger treatment effect than the one observed, and the event rate in
the control group was lower than anticipated, reflecting the excellence
of contemporary secondary prevention. The open design was unavoidable,
and although outcome adjudication was blinded, referral for
hospitalisation could in principle have been influenced by knowledge of
the assignment. Finally, the enrolled population was relatively young
and predominantly male, and the findings should be extrapolated with
caution to older patients and to women.

\section{Conclusion}
Among patients entering cardiac rehabilitation after myocardial
infarction, a twelve-week programme of high-intensity interval training
improved cardiorespiratory fitness more than standard moderate-intensity
continuous training and was associated with a nominally lower rate of
the composite clinical endpoint that did not reach statistical
significance. Serious adverse events were uncommon in both groups. The
findings support the safety of HIIT delivered at multicentre scale and
justify a larger, event-driven trial to determine whether the suggested
clinical benefit is real.
\end{document}

instruction: 这篇心脏康复随机对照试验还没有摘要。通读全文后，在 \maketitle 之后加上 abstract 环境写一段结构化程度适中的英文摘要，覆盖：研究背景与缺口、设计（多中心随机对照）、样本量、主要终点结果（带上关键数字）和结论，单段不超过 200 词。正文一个字都不要动。

grader.rubric: 5: 摘要位于 \maketitle 后的 abstract 环境内、单段 ≤200 词，准确覆盖背景/多中心随机设计/样本量 612/主要终点（23\% 相对降低且未达显著）/随访 18 months/安全性（4.2\% vs 6.1\%），数字与 Results 一致，语言凝练专业，正文无改动；4: 要素齐全但漏写 1 个关键数字或略微超词数；3: 写了摘要但漏 2 个关键数字，或数字与 Results 有出入，或明显超词数；2: 摘要流于空泛口号、基本无具体数字，或擅自改动正文；1: 未写摘要或写错位置，或编造文中没有的数据
